sentences.text: Elmisaurus rarus lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in Asia.
Although the fossils are incomplete, the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is estimated to have reached a body length of 1.68 meters.
Like all oviraptorosaurs, this animal was a feathered, warm-blooded biped.
Its foot was light and slender, measuring about 15 centimeters in length.
The hand was roughly 20 centimeters long and slender, featuring bone shafts that were much narrower than the ends, a trait unique among oviraptorosaurs.
Claws on the hand were strongly curved.
The name Elmisaurus means "foot sole" because the type specimen consisted of a metatarsus.
This species is the first discovered caenagnathid for which both hands and feet are known.
Two fragmentary specimens of a small theropod were found in 1970 by a Polish-Mongolian expedition in the Ömnögovĭ province of Mongolia.
Halszka Osmólska formally described Elmisaurus rarus in 1981.
The paratype specimen ZPAL MgD-I/20 is one-fifth longer than the holotype.
Evidence from the fossils suggests the forehead bones formed a high crest that continued through the nose.
The vertebrae were highly pneumatized.
The shoulder joint directed outward and downward.
The first finger was slender.
A bump on the top surface of the fourth metatarsal protruded over the fifth metatarsal bone and rose above the midfoot joint surface.
A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues examined 23 foot bones referred to Elmisaurus for stress fractures but found none.
A 2013 analysis by Longrich et al. classified Elmisaurus as a caenagnathid.
A 2007 analysis by Senter places Elmisaurus with Chirostenotes and Hagryphus, distinct from Avimimus.
Elmisaurus lived from 72.2 to 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
In 1997, Hans-Dieter Sues argued that the second species should be referred to Chirostenotes, a view not accepted by Philip J. Currie.
Elmisaurus was previously considered a relative of Chirostenotes within Elmisauridae and later Caenagnathidae, but this relationship was questioned by Maryanska et al. in 2002.
While a relationship with Avimimus is possible, a 2007 analysis by Senter places Elmisaurus with Chirostenotes and Hagryphus, far from Avimimus.
